articles.title: Tesla Begins Inviting Customers to Purchase Cybercab Robotaxi
articles.summary: Tesla has begun inviting select customers to purchase its Cybercab robotaxi, which requires a monthly autonomy subscription and comes with strict usage restrictions.
articles.content: Tesla has begun inviting select customers to purchase its Cybercab, a steering-wheel-less robotaxi designed for personal use and ride-hailing services. The Cybercab comes in two packages: an initial purchase price of $29,990, plus a monthly "autonomy subscription that costs $299. This is not just an optional feature, but a requirement to operate the vehicle at all. According to Tesla's Cybercab order and subscription agreements, which were made public over the weekend, the autonomous EV will not function without a valid autonomy subscription in place. In essence, this means owners who fail to pay the monthly fee risk having their vehicle rendered useless. Those who do receive an invite to purchase a Cybercab will be limited to using it within specific areas designated for Tesla's Robotaxi ride-hailing service. Currently, these areas include parts of Texas and Florida, such as Austin, Dallas, Miami, Orlando, and Tampa. The fine print of Tesla's Cybercab subscription agreement reveals some surprising conditions for owners who fail to pay the $299 monthly fee. If a customer defaults on their payment, they face a hefty penalty of $50,000. But that's not all - Tesla also reserves the right to remotely disable the vehicle, essentially turning it into an expensive paperweight. The company can repurchase the Cybercab at any time, with the price determined by its own valuation, but there's no guarantee that owners will get a replacement vehicle. Other terms of the agreement include restrictions on modifying the Cybercab, including adding wraps or tinted windows. This means owners won't be able to personalize their vehicles as they see fit. Tesla is also collecting data from Cybercab owners, which will be used to improve the product and provide ride support. The company will have access to personally identifying information such as location data and images recorded by a camera above the rear-view mirror, but it's unclear whether owners can opt out of this data collection. Tesla's Cybercab is set to become a subscription-only vehicle, marking a significant shift in the company's business model towards tech-driven revenue streams. The decision follows Musk's announcement earlier this month that Tesla would discontinue the Cybertruck, after previously phasing out the Model S and X earlier this year. This move underscores Tesla's focus on autonomous driving technologies, as hinted at by Musk's vision for future revenue sources. Notably, early invitees to order the Cybercab include tech reviewer Marques Brownlee, who had been skeptical about Tesla's ability to deliver a sub-$30,000 Cybercab by 2026. However, after receiving his confirmed order, he shared a screenshot on social media and expressed relief that his hair was safe. The Cybercab's geofencing limitations mean it can only be used in specific locations, falling short of Musk's promise for personal robotaxis. When taken home, Brownlee quipped that the vehicle would become a paperweight." articles.title: Blanket Coats Take Center Stage in Fashion Collections
articles.summary: Designers like Colleen Allen and TWP are showcasing oversized scarf shawls turned into coats on their fall/winter 2026 runways.
articles.content: The latest trend in fashion is all about wraps, shawls, and capes that serve as elevated versions of blanket coats. At the forefront of this trend are designers like Colleen Allen and TWP who showcased supersized scarf shawls turned into coats on their fall/winter 2026 runways. The oversized designs were draped elegantly over models, exuding a sense of comfort and warmth. These wearable wraps have become a staple in many fashion collections. But what sets the blanket coat apart from other winter staples? For one, it offers a unique feel that's more about wrapping oneself in warmth than making a bold statement like a black puffer jacket might. The blanket coat has also taken on a symbolic significance, representing both physical and metaphorical well-being in today's chaotic world. Models at Fforme walked the runway draped in huge swaths of furry fabrics that enveloped them completely, evoking images of being swaddled. At Khaite, dresses were styled with large cocooning blanket-like throws trailing off the backs, adding to the overall sense of warmth and comfort. Designers are embracing comfort as a core theme in their collections, blurring the lines between practicality and whimsy. The blanket coat has become a staple in many designers' visions, often styled to resemble a cozy throw wrapped around one's shoulders. This trend is not unlike taking a piece of home with you on-the-go, bringing a sense of familiarity and warmth to the outside world. In show notes for TWP's fall/winter 2026 collection, founder Trish Wescoat Pound referenced inviting elements like hot toddies, jigsaw puzzles, and fireplaces alongside warm fabrics such as Scottish cashmere. The blanket coat has become a staple in many fashion collections, with smaller brands like LilyEve offering unique takes on the trend. These brands are able to create one-of-a-kind pieces by upcycling vintage materials, such as hand-sourced Hermès blankets. articles.title: Trans individuals find new ways to express themselves through affordable fashion swaps
articles.summary: Clothing swaps provide a sense of safety and community for marginalized communities.
articles.content: Trans individuals across the United States are finding new ways to express themselves through clothing swaps, which provide not only affordable fashion but also a sense of safety and community. For those who attend these events, like Isaiah Kirk in Chicago, it's about more than just picking out a trendy outfit - it's about embracing their identity without fear of judgment or rejection. Kirk recently left the Uncommon Closet with a stylish combination of jeans and a Pokémon graphic tee, all for free. Kirk identifies as nonbinary and transmasculine, and like many others in similar circumstances, finds solace in clothing that allows them to express themselves authentically. As anti-trans legislation continues to be implemented nationwide, these gatherings have become crucial for fostering a sense of belonging among marginalized communities. AJ Mix, who runs community outreach at the Uncommon Closet, has seen firsthand the impact of these events on clients struggling with body dysmorphia or dysphoria. Many are trans or queer individuals who've faced discrimination for not conforming to societal expectations surrounding their assigned sex at birth. The Uncommon Closet's mission is not just about providing clothes, but also a sense of safety and comfort for those who need it most. According to Mix, their clients often come from traumatic experiences related to shopping, making even simple tasks like buying clothes a daunting task. As a result, Mix offers a therapeutic approach to personal styling, often accompanying clients on trips to stores that may be intimidating or overwhelming without support. This personalized service is particularly important for trans women who are early in their transition and may not feel comfortable navigating traditional shopping environments alone. Mix initially planned the Uncommon Closet's clothing swap as a one-time event during its grand reopening in 2024, but the high demand for this free service prompted them to expand it into a regular occurrence. Today, they host three swaps per year, tailored to Chicago's seasonal weather shifts: spring, summer, and winter. The popularity of Mix's clothing swaps can be attributed in part to the influx of individuals from the South moving to Chicago due to the changing political climate. This demographic shift has created a need for accessible and inclusive services like the Uncommon Closet's. The Uncommon Closet's founder has witnessed firsthand the joy of scoring a binder at one of their clothing swaps, where attendees can take home gently used items for free. These meetups are not just about acquiring new clothes, but also about building connections and finding a sense of belonging within the trans community. Carroll notes that often people arrive alone but leave with new friends and a stronger connection to their community. The need for accessible services like these clothing swaps is underscored by Christabell Nunez, who wanted to create a safe space in Austin where marginalized individuals of all body sizes could explore fashion without judgment or scrutiny. The clothes swaps are designed to be a take-what-you-need affair, with participants encouraged to help themselves to as much clothing as they can use without restriction. However, there is one caveat: attendees are asked not to resell the donated items for profit. Librarians are also getting in on the action, recognizing that these swaps provide an opportunity to promote inclusivity and diversity within their communities. For instance, at a library's first swap event, a refugee mother was able to find new clothes for her children after fleeing her home country with only two suitcases of belongings. In Texas, where anti-trans laws have been proposed in large numbers, including the highest number in the United States in 2021, librarians are working hard to ensure that their programming and literature is inclusive. This includes making a conscious effort to showcase diverse voices and perspectives. Meanwhile, on the other side of the state line in Tennessee, Jack Knoxville had his own reasons for starting a clothing swap back in 2016: he felt there was a lack of positive representation for trans individuals in his home state, which only exacerbated existing feelings of marginalization. Clothing swaps are not just about exchanging old clothes for new ones; they're also about building confidence and resilience in trans individuals. For those who participate, the experience can be transformative, equipping them with essential items for daily life, such as warm clothing for winter months or professional attire for job interviews. The impact of these swaps is profound, with participants often reporting feelings of euphoria and empowerment, much like getting a fresh haircut. This sense of confidence can stay with individuals long after the swap ends, helping them navigate challenging situations with greater ease. By sharing their expertise, Knoxville has empowered others to host similar events in their own cities, fostering a culture of creativity and resourcefulness within trans communities. articles.title: Thanksgiving Travel Expected to Decline Slightly This Year
articles.summary: A slight decline in Thanksgiving travel is expected this year due to rising costs of airfare and gasoline.
articles.content: A slight decline in Thanksgiving travel is expected this year due to rising costs of airfare and gasoline, according to a forecast by AAA. The predicted decrease is estimated at 121,000 fewer travelers compared to last year's numbers, which translates to a one-tenth of a percent drop. This would mark the end of three consecutive years of record-breaking Thanksgiving travel, a trend that followed the COVID-19 pandemic. AAA's annual forecast suggests that despite higher travel costs, airport security lines and highway traffic are unlikely to see significant changes. The transportation infrastructure is expected to function smoothly by the time Thanksgiving travel season begins, according to officials at the Department of Transportation and the Federal Aviation Administration. A spokesperson for AAA suggests that last week's extended ground stop may not significantly impact holiday travel unless a similar disruption occurs again, implying that travelers are accustomed to adapting to unexpected setbacks. Travelers, it appears, have shown remarkable resilience in the face of adversity, with many willing to brave higher costs and other challenges in order to reach their destinations during peak travel periods. As has been the case in previous years, a significant majority of holiday travelers are expected to opt for road trips over flying, despite rising fuel prices that will make gasoline more expensive than it was last year. The ongoing tensions in the Middle East, particularly the war with Iran, are a concern that may weigh on travelers' minds this Thanksgiving season. A contributing factor to Americans' caution is the lingering inflation that influenced the midterm elections earlier this month. Rising costs have made some people more hesitant to take long trips for their holiday meals. Air travel costs are also expected to be a significant burden, with airfares significantly higher than last year due in part to airlines spending more on jet fuel. Additionally, carriers have increased fees for checked bags, making the overall cost of flying even steeper. With Thanksgiving travel expected to dip slightly due to higher prices, about 12,000 fewer people are predicted to hit the roads and skies compared to last year's numbers, according to AAA estimates. The organization forecasts that between November 24th and 30th, there will be a noticeable decrease in travel. Theme parks and cruise vacations have long been major draws for visitors to Florida during this time of year, with Detroit and Dallas also making the top 10 list due to their hosting of Thanksgiving football games. Other organizations reviewing similar data have proposed varying projections, but one thing is certain: travelers are facing a more expensive holiday season than in years past. articles.title: Thailand Luxury Hotel Market Sees Significant Revenue Growth
articles.summary: Minor Hotels' high-end properties in Thailand reported a 19% increase in RevPAR during the third quarter.
articles.content: Thailand's luxury hotel market is bucking the trend of declining tourist numbers, with Minor Hotels reporting a significant increase in revenue per available room (RevPAR) for its high-end properties in the country. According to Minor's quarterly results statement, Anantara-branded hotels in Thailand experienced a 19% like-for-like rise in RevPAR during the third quarter, driven by a 13% increase in average daily rate. This performance was particularly notable given that overall tourist numbers in Thailand are down, with international arrivals forecast to reach only 33 million by 2026, down from an earlier estimate of 36.7 million. The resilience of luxury hotel bookings in Thailand is attributed to the fact that high-end guests are less price sensitive than those in other segments of the market. This insight was shared by Cushman & Wakefield, which pointed out that luxury hotels tend to perform better during times of economic uncertainty. Minor's Thai properties not only led the way in terms of revenue growth but also contributed significantly to the company's overall performance during the quarter. With core profit rising 13% year over year to THB 2.1 billion (approximately $62.9 million), Minor's results were boosted by strong performances from other markets, including the Maldives and Europe. The company's core revenue grew 6% to THB 35.4 billion (about $1.06 billion) during the quarter, while earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) rose 4% to THB 7 billion (approximately $210 million). Minor's RevPAR across all markets increased by 5%, largely driven by rate gains. Minor Hotels' ownership structure, which sees it owning most of its hotels in Thailand, also played a key role in its financial performance during the quarter. This allowed the company to reap the benefits of rate increases directly in its results, contributing to its overall revenue growth. Minor's recent investments in Thailand have clearly paid off, contributing significantly to its overall revenue growth. The company has made substantial improvements to its luxury properties in the region, including a $50 million renovation of Anantara Siam Bangkok, which was completed in September. All 335 rooms at the hotel were refurbished, as well as its restaurants and event spaces. The upgraded facilities are expected to boost bookings and revenue for the property. Meanwhile, Minor's resorts in the Maldives have also seen an uptick in performance, with RevPAR rising by 10% due to increased occupancy levels. Although rates fell slightly, the improved occupancy has helped drive revenue growth for the company. In contrast, Minor's hotels in the Middle East and Africa region experienced a decline in RevPAR, falling by 11% in the third quarter. This was largely due to lower occupancy levels, which decreased by around three points, as well as reduced rates, which fell by about 5%. The regional conflict has been cited as a major factor contributing to weaker travel demand. Minor's strategy of protecting prices rather than chasing volume is being put to the test in the region. Despite efforts to maintain rates, Minor reported that its Gulf hotels saw rates fall for the first time this year in the third quarter. Minor International's exposure to the Middle East is a significant concern given the region's downturn in tourism. With about 40% of its hotels in this region owned directly, any decline in occupancy and rates affects Minor's bottom line more than it would for other chains that rely on management fees. The Middle East slump has had a direct impact on Minor's earnings, with four out of every ten hotels in the region experiencing the effects. This is because Minor owns or leases a higher proportion of its hotels in this region compared to its overall portfolio. The company's lighter exposure to the Middle East, however, may be a blessing in disguise. In contrast, Europe and the Americas have seen a surge in demand for hotel rooms. NH Hotels in Minor's portfolio reported a 7% increase in revenue per available room (RevPAR) during the seasonally strongest quarter of the year. The cities of Madrid and Barcelona led the charge, with occupancy rates up by 11% and 8%, respectively. East Africa also showed signs of growth, with Kenya and Tanzania reporting a 5% increase in RevPAR. Meanwhile, Australia and New Zealand maintained high occupancy levels, holding steady at 80%. These positive trends have helped to offset some of the losses experienced by Minor's hotels in other regions. Minor's core profit for the first nine months of the year rose by 3% to THB 4.2 billion ($126 million), with the third quarter accounting for half of that total. The company is now looking ahead to mixed trading conditions in the fourth quarter, with forward bookings for Thailand and the Maldives outpacing last year's figures for both this period and early 2027. Minor International's diversified portfolio has proven to be a key factor in its resilience during a period of uneven trading conditions, according to Dillip Rajakarier, group CEO. The company will prioritize protecting margins and maintaining pricing discipline while accelerating the shift towards fee income, as evident from its pipeline. A significant proportion of Minor's active development pipeline consists of asset-light arrangements, with 38 hotels signed in the first nine months alone. This strategy is expected to continue even after new properties open, as Minor's results will remain tied to the performance of markets where it owns existing buildings, such as Europe and the Middle East. articles.title: US Foreign Student Enrollment Falls 9% This Fall
articles.summary: A significant decline in foreign students studying at US universities has been reported, coinciding with the Trump administration's immigration crackdown and changes to higher education policies.
articles.content: A significant decline in foreign students studying at US universities has been reported, coinciding with the Trump administration's immigration crackdown and changes to higher education policies. According to a survey by the Institute of International Education, international enrollment on US campuses fell by 9% this fall compared to last year, while new student arrivals decreased by 15%. Veena Dubal, general counsel for the American Association of University Professors, recalls her father's experience as an international student at Tuskegee University in the late 1960s. She notes that it was a time when opportunities were available for students like him to pursue education and work temporarily in the US. The decline in foreign students may be attributed in part to proposed regulations requiring schools to pay a $70,000 fee for each student participating in the Optional Practical Training (OPT) program, which allows international students to gain temporary work experience after graduating. The decline in foreign students studying at US universities is attributed to a range of factors beyond politics. According to college leaders who spoke to the Institute of International Education (IIE), even though the US remains the top destination for international students globally, changes are having an impact on enrollment numbers. A significant portion of colleges and universities surveyed this fall pointed to two main culprits: the visa application process and travel restrictions. Eighty-eight percent blamed the former, while 70% cited the latter as reasons for the decline in foreign student enrollment. Other factors contributing to the decline include students' concerns about research funding, according to Mirka Martel, head of research, evaluation and learning at the IIE. Fanta Aw, executive director and CEO of NAFSA, an association representing international education, also noted that changes in federal grant-giving processes have made students wary of pursuing degrees in the US. The decline in foreign students enrolling at US universities has been attributed to concerns over uncertainty in the country's policies and procedures. Students are weighing their options carefully, taking into account the complexity of navigating the US education system and considering alternative destinations with fewer bureaucratic hurdles. Cleveland State University is one institution feeling the pinch, with international enrollment plummeting by 46% in just two years, from 1,542 students in fall 2025 to 828 this autumn. The budgetary implications are significant, with Provost Nigamanth Sridhar estimating that the loss of tuition revenue could range between $2 million and $4 million. International graduate enrollment has taken a significant hit this fall, plummeting by 15% compared to last year. In contrast, undergraduate international student numbers have decreased by a relatively modest 3%. Congressional oversight might offer some stability for international students in the short term, according to Sarah Spreitzer of the American Council on Education. She notes that targeted policies and oversight could provide much-needed certainty for these students. As she pointed out, such measures could prevent sudden or unexplainable changes from affecting their ability to study in the US. articles.title: 80% of employees feel more productive from AI. Only 37% of companies see it in profit
articles.summary: A staggering 80% of employees worldwide claim that AI has significantly improved their productivity levels, yet a significant disparity exists between this perceived value and actual profitability for companies.
articles.content: A staggering 80% of employees worldwide claim that AI has significantly improved their productivity levels, yet a significant disparity exists between this perceived value and actual profitability for companies. While many organisations are reaping the benefits of AI in terms of enhanced employee performance, only a mere 37% have seen a tangible impact on their bottom line. The disconnect between perceived value and actual financial gain is puzzling, given that most businesses have access to the data needed to make informed decisions. However, it appears that knowing what needs to be done and actually taking action are two distinct challenges that organisations face daily. A closer examination of various industries reveals a common theme: valuable insights often go unrealised due to inertia. In many cases, constraints on value realisation stem not from rigid rules but from outdated decisions that have become entrenched over time. These decisions can be revisited and revised to unlock new potential, empowering employees to drive meaningful change within their organisations. As someone who has led global industry teams and spearheaded strategic business transformations at a tech giant, I've witnessed firsthand the difficulties companies face in extracting value from AI investments. Many businesses struggle to bridge the gap between perceived benefits and actual financial returns on investment. One notable example involves a large aviation partner that invested heavily in an AI-powered solution to optimise crew scheduling, aircraft rotation, passenger management, and ground control. Despite having a strong sponsor and access to significant resources, the project stalled due to conflicting opinions and entrenched attitudes within the organisation. The case highlights the need for organisations to revisit their decision-making processes and address deeply ingrained patterns of thinking that hinder value realisation. By doing so, businesses can unlock the full potential of AI and translate perceived benefits into tangible financial gains. The airline's AI implementation had shown remarkable results, but its full potential was hindered by the cautious approach of decision-makers. It took 18 months for them to transition from accepting half of the AI's recommendations to almost all, a testament to the system's value. However, this progress stalled when it came to expanding the AI across the entire network. The fear of an AI model overruling decades of experience and established practices held back the implementation process. This wasn't due to doubts about the AI's worth but rather a constraint that resides within people, not the system itself. Companies can reap the benefits of AI while still maintaining control over decision-making processes. By automating analysis, they can make more informed choices without sacrificing corporate politics. One client recently showcased their dynamic pricing model with pride, only to reveal the constraints they had imposed upon it. The model's ability to recommend changes is one thing, but actual approval lies elsewhere, in the bonus plan. A decade ago at Diageo, a similar approach was taken by combining various data points such as sell-out, sentiment, media spend, and weather data for each brand and country. When Ireland's rugby team won, sales of Guinness increased significantly on TV, outperforming other markets where the plan was initially built. Conversely, when the sun stayed in Italy, Tanqueray saw a boost in sales during its season. This was simply a matter of math, but every euro moved had real-world consequences for country managers and their bonuses. Ultimately, the AI tool remained a lagging indicator of what could have been achieved if more decisive action were taken. The benefits of AI are clear, but unlocking them requires navigating the complexities of human decision-making processes. The benefits of AI are clear, but unlocking them requires navigating the complexities of human decision-making processes. This paradox is reflected in the numbers: 80% of employees report feeling more productive thanks to AI, yet only 37% of companies have seen a profit from its implementation. When AI takes over routine tasks, it frees up time for employees to focus on higher-value work. However, this shift can be unsettling for those whose roles are being automated. It's as if they're watching their own redundancy being drafted. The challenges posed by AI are not limited to the individual level; entire companies must also adapt to its implications. At Maersk, a major shipping company, the industry was once unprofitable, but the introduction of integrated logistics helped turn things around during the pandemic. Last year, the company earned $3.5 billion in operating profit. Leaders have a crucial role to play in helping employees see the potential benefits of AI and how they can contribute to it. However, this requires more than just technical expertise, it demands an understanding of human psychology and behavior. A recent conversation with an executive assistant highlighted the importance of recognizing individual value in the face of technological change. She was concerned that her use of AI would make her redundant, but when asked about a time she felt proud of her contribution, she revealed a different story. She had brought together a leadership team with strong personalities and helped them work towards a common goal. Her role wasn't just to complete tasks; it was to create an environment where they could collaborate effectively. If AI were ever able to replicate this kind of interpersonal skill, she would be the one to train it, and it would allow her to scale her impact like never before. The key challenge facing employees is not the technology itself, but rather recognizing their own value in a world where tasks are being automated. This requires a deeper understanding of what makes each person unique and how they can contribute to the organization's success. Ultimately, the future of work with AI will depend on our ability to navigate these complexities and create an environment where humans and machines can work together effectively. The disparity between productivity and profitability in AI adoption is striking, with 80% of employees claiming increased efficiency from artificial intelligence yet only 37% of companies seeing a financial return on investment. This discrepancy highlights the limitations of relying solely on technology to drive growth, as the economy continues to evolve around its next constraint. For centuries, humans have pushed boundaries by acquiring more resources, building new infrastructure, or expanding their workforce. However, with AI, the challenge has shifted to navigating human capabilities and limitations. To bridge this gap, four key strategies can help organisations overcome the hurdles associated with integrating AI into their operations. The first step is to set ambitious yet achievable goals that inspire employees to think beyond current constraints. By focusing on long-term objectives, teams are encouraged to innovate and adapt rather than merely optimising existing processes. Organisations must also conduct a thorough review of their internal rules and narratives to identify outdated or limiting assumptions. This involves asking questions about the origins of each constraint and whether they remain relevant in today's environment. By acknowledging and addressing these internal barriers, companies can create an environment conducive to AI adoption. Ultimately, successful AI implementation requires more than just budgetary adjustments; it demands a fundamental shift in how organisations operate and measure success. By incorporating elements that promote shared ownership and accountability, leaders can foster a culture of collaboration and innovation. As leaders strive to harness the potential of artificial intelligence, a striking disparity emerges between employee productivity and company profitability. Despite 80% of employees reporting increased productivity from AI adoption, only about one-third of companies are seeing tangible financial benefits. The disconnect highlights the importance of fostering a culture that enables collaboration and innovation. By making the first honest move towards incorporating shared ownership and accountability elements, leaders can create momentum within their organisations and drive meaningful change.
